name: PT Yanaprima Hastapersada Tbk

frontmatter.title: Yanaprima Hastapersada — a cyclical packaging converter priced ahead of its export wave
frontmatter.summary: YPAS is a polypropylene woven-bags producer in East Java. H1 2026 margins jumped on Asian export shipments, but the company's base-rate gross margin sits in the high single digits, not near a fifth, and the price pays a rich multiple on both earnings and enterprise value for a converter whose normalised ROIC equals its WACC. A thin free float draws a liquidity discount.
thesis: H1 2026 export shipments lifted gross margin above the FY2025A average as plastic-bag and roll-sheet lines took higher-priced Asian orders, notably to Lucky Star Weaving Co Ltd [S8][S6].
The structural margin is under pressure from intense domestic cement-bag competition and import-driven raw-material price swings; our fade follows the company's own risk statement [S6].
The DCF value of Rp376 per share sits well below the Rp765 price, which pays a high multiple on both earnings and enterprise value before adjusting for the free‑float discount [S0].

The public holding is 10.2% on the company register and the market data pack estimates the free float slightly lower; the fund's published liquidity schedule, not a judgement about this name, prices the illiquidity of a stock trading this thinly at 20.0% of the target [S0].

catalysts.event: Renewal or replacement of the BRI working-capital facility that matured on 4 October 2026
FY2026 full-year results — the second-half bottom line will confirm whether H1 2026's profit is repeatable
Q3 2026 LK filing — first read on whether the H1 inventory build unwinds into sales or a write-down

blocks.text: We rate PT Yanaprima Hastapersada Tbk (YPAS) **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp299**, -60.9% against the Rp765 close. YPAS converts polypropylene resin into woven plastic bags, laminated sacks, cement-bag kraft-paper composites, roll sheet and sandwich sheet, and PP woven block-bottom bags [S6].

The call rests on the margin fade, not the top line. H1 2026 net sales of IDR196.4bn rose from IDR171.9bn a year earlier, with exports at IDR44.1bn [S8]. That export wave drove a gross margin well above the FY2025A 8.9% base, with plastic bags and roll sheet earning margins above a fifth while cement bags barely broke even [S8][S7]. But the three audited fiscal years ran at 11.1%, 7.2% and 8.9%, an average below ten per cent [S6], the company flags intense price competition for plastic sacks, and the cement-bag segment has no pricing power [S6][S7]. A sustained margin above that band is the upside, not the base case.

The valuation gap comes from the price paying a high multiple on both enterprise value and earnings for a converter whose normalised ROIC sits around its cost of capital. The primary DCF values the equity at Rp376 per share, a large discount to the market. The company register shows a public holding of 10.2% [S2], against the 9.1% free-float estimate in the market data pack [S0]; the difference is the two commissioner holdings and the vendor's treatment of the block. The target line then carries the fund's published liquidity schedule (fund rules `coverage.liquidity_discount`), a step haircut keyed to average daily traded value and standing here at 20.0%; the discount rate carries no separate illiquidity premium, the COE premium line being 0.0%, so the adjustment is explicit and visible rather than buried in the WACC [S0].

What would change the view: a second half that holds the H1 margin on a stable export mix, a disclosed long-term export contract, or evidence that the BRI facility has been renewed on comparable terms. Three things move the value — the gross margin, the working-capital drag (NWC is IDR130.4bn against revenue of IDR362.4bn [S7]), and the discount rate; the sensitivity table in the valuation section sizes them.

PT Yanaprima Hastapersada Tbk runs a single production site in Sidoarjo, East Java, making woven-plastic packaging for the cement, sugar, fertilizer, rice and general-industrial sectors [S6]. The business was founded in 1995, began producing plastic sacks (woven bags) in 1997 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in March 2008 [S6]. It added laminated sacks in 2000, cement bags in 2005 and the PP woven block-bottom bag in 2009 [S6]. The current portfolio spans four reportable segments: plastic bags (IDR159bn FY2025A net sales), cement bags (IDR132bn), roll sheet and sandwich sheet (IDR68bn) and other lines (IDR3bn) [S7].

The company does not publish capacity in tonnes, but FY2025A production reached 93.7% of the year's target [S6]. Management set a FY2026E sales target of IDR380.0bn, net profit of IDR5.5bn and 75% machine utilisation [S6]; H1 2026 revenue of IDR196.4bn has already overtaken half of that sales target [S8]. The workforce was 1,023 employees at end-FY2025A [S6].

Revenue by geography: domestic sales were IDR308bn and exports IDR54bn in FY2025A [S6]. In H1 2026 exports rose to IDR44.1bn, or about a fifth of net sales [S8]. The export push goes to East Asia, South Asia, West Asia and ASEAN, and increasingly the Americas [S6][S8]. The largest H1 2026 customer was Lucky Star Weaving Co Ltd at IDR35.7bn, or 18.2% of net sales [S8].

The mix shifted sharply in H1 2026: plastic bags and roll sheet grew while cement bags fell, and the segment gross margins diverged just as sharply, with plastic bags and roll sheet above a fifth and cement bags barely positive [S8]. Related-party sales to PT Forindoprima Perkasa and PT Yanasurya Bhaktipersada were IDR19.0bn in H1 2026, or 9.7% of net sales [S8]. The controlling shareholder is PT Hastagraha Bumipersada at 89.5%; the public holding is 10.2% [S2].

YPAS is a challenger in a fragmented Indonesian woven-bag market rather than a price leader. Its differentiator is the breadth of the product range and the dual domestic-export footprint; its constraint is that cement bags, the second segment by revenue, earn almost nothing at the margin [S8][S7].

Polypropylene resin is a commodity derived from oil cracking. It is formed into yarn, woven into cloth, laminated with BOPP film and cut and sewn into sacks. The cement-bag variety sandwiches a paper layer between two woven PP sheets; roll sheet and sandwich sheet are intermediate packaging materials; the block-bottom bag is a bottom-gusseted sack used for cement and flour. Imported resin dominates the raw-material cost, and Indonesian producers compete with imports of finished sacks from the wider ASEAN region.

The Indonesian plastics industry grew about 8.5% in 2025, and plastic-sack demand rose in both the domestic market and exports, with sugar, rice and fertilizer packaging the main domestic outlets [S6]. Domestic economic growth was 5.11% in 2025 [S6]. The macro deck carries Indonesian real GDP growth of 5.3%, CPI of 3.3% and a rupiah at 19,000 to the dollar in the long run [S0].

The woven-bag market is fragmented and price-competitive. Cement-bag demand tracks domestic cement consumption, which has been soft: the company's cement-bag segment revenue fell 21.2% in FY2025A [S6] and its H1 2026 gross margin was barely positive [S8]. Plastic-bag and roll-sheet demand for food and general packaging grows with population and income, but cheap imported sacks and resin-price volatility keep the sector's returns low [S6]. The company's own risk statement names polypropylene resin-price fluctuation as the dominant business risk: PP is a commodity whose price is set by global supply and demand, with Indonesia importing from ASEAN, South Asia, East Asia and the Middle East [S6].

Five forces for YPAS: - **Buyer power** is high. Cement producers such as PT Semen Baturaja (5.3% of H1 2026 net sales) and sugar mills have many suppliers and buy a commodity [S8]. - **Supplier power** is moderate. PP resin is imported and a handful of suppliers matter: PT PCM Kimia Indonesia accounted for 7.5% of H1 2026 cost of sales [S8]. - **New entrants** are a moderate threat; spinning and weaving lines are capital-intensive but the technology is not proprietary. - **Substitutes** include kraft paper bags for cement and flexible pouches for food-grade packaging. - **Rivalry** is intense; the company itself cites "persaingan harga yang ketat" (intense price competition) in plastic sacks [S6], and the cement-bag segment's barely positive H1 2026 gross margin shows how little pricing power survives [S8].

YPAS's moat is thin: operating experience since 1997, a diversified product range and an export channel that lifted pricing in FY2025A and H1 2026 [S6][S8]. The export channel is real but concentrated in one customer, and the domestic cement-bag business has no pricing power. Market share is not disclosed; the company is a mid-sized converter, not a leader.

The industry's economics are set by the spread between resin cost and bag price rather than by volume. Both sides of that spread are negotiated with larger counterparties — resin suppliers on the import side and cement and sugar producers on the domestic side — so a converter earns a normal return only when it can differentiate on specification, delivery reliability or export relationships [S6]. The H1 2026 result is consistent with two transmissions, and the filings do not let us separate them: export orders may have carried better prices than the domestic book, or the margin gain may come from resin cost and a mix shift into roll sheet, the highest-margin segment in the interim accounts [S8]. We treat the export-price story as an inference, not a disclosed fact — the company reports export revenue and segment gross profit but no export/domestic margin split [S8]. The two readings fade differently: a price premium erodes when competing exporters undercut, while a resin-cost gain reverses when the resin price normalises. Our base case fades the margin on the first channel and checks the second in the risk section. The domestic cement business ran at close to cost [S8], which explains why the industry consolidates slowly and why the listed peer set is small: returns are low and cyclical, and the capital needed to add capacity is not rewarded with pricing power.

Regulation and external influences are light compared with commodity producers: there is no price control or royalty regime. FX matters because resin is dollar-priced and exports are dollar-earning; the rupiah is assumed at 19,000 long run [S0].

Revenue is forecast from the FY2025A base of IDR362.4bn with growth of 10.0% in FY2026E, then 5.0% fading to 3.0% by FY2030E. The FY2026E revenue line of IDR398.6bn is above, not below, the company's own IDR380.0bn target [S6], because H1 2026 net sales of IDR196.4bn were already just over half that target and exports were running at IDR44.1bn [S8]. The other half of that guidance is stale: the IDR5.5bn net profit target was set before H1 2026 produced IDR15.6bn of net profit, more than double the full-year plan [S6][S8], so we do not anchor the forecast to it. The growth is export-led: FY2025A exports were 54 IDR bn against a decline in domestic sales [S6][S7].

Gross margin is the key assumption. H1 2026 gross profit was IDR35.8bn on net sales of IDR196.4bn [S8], against 8.9% for FY2025A, 7.2% for FY2024A and 11.1% for FY2023A [S6][S7]. By segment, plastic bags earned IDR20.0bn of gross profit on IDR92.8bn of sales, roll sheet IDR12.5bn on IDR52.5bn, and cement bags only IDR0.6bn on IDR47.2bn [S8]. The base case carries 18.2% for FY2026E — the H1 2026 actual, not a haircut — and then fades to 16.0% by FY2030E. The fade is sourced, not assumed: the company flags intense price competition [S6], the cement-bag segment earns almost nothing at the gross line [S8], and the three audited fiscal years ran at 11.1%, 7.2% and 8.9% [S6]. Even the FY2030E level sits above that history, which is the respect the export mix deserves.

Costs. Operating expense was IDR25.1bn in FY2025A [S7]. We hold the opex ratio at 7.5% in FY2026E, close to the H1 2026 ratio [S8], and 7.3% thereafter because operating leverage is limited in this business. The tax rate is set at 22.0%, the Indonesian statutory rate [S8]; the FY2025A effective rate was near zero only because pre-tax profit was small [S7].

Cash flow and the restatement. The data pack's D&A is a fraction of the real charge because Indonesian financial statements use the direct cash-flow method. We restate D&A from the LK notes to IDR14.0bn for FY2024A and IDR14.5bn for FY2025A [S7]. That lifts FY2025A EBITDA to IDR21.9bn from the IDR7.3bn EBIT line [S7]. The restatement covers the two fiscal years that feed the model; FY2022A and FY2023A still carry the pack's nominal D&A, and they are not used downstream because the DCF starts in FY2026E. FY2025A operating cash flow was IDR41.5bn [S7]; it benefited from a working-capital release (NWC fell to IDR130.4bn from IDR151.3bn [S7]). The H1 2026 accounts show the reverse, with inventory rising to IDR91.5bn and operating cash flow turning negative despite the IDR15.6bn net profit [S8]. Working capital is large for the size of the business: NWC is IDR130.4bn on revenue of IDR362.4bn, and the forecast holds the ratio at 35.9%, the FY2025A actual [S7].

Balance sheet. Net debt was IDR50.6bn at end-FY2025A, or 2.3x EBITDA [S7]. At 30 June 2026 the company held cash of IDR14.3bn, short-term bank debt of IDR71.6bn and a separate IDR50.0bn non-interest-bearing loan from the controlling shareholder [S8]; the bank debt, not the shareholder loan, is what we treat as debt in the valuation bridge. The bank-borrowings note of the interim accounts sets out the security: the BCA facilities are secured on land and buildings, receivables and inventory "dan jaminan perusahaan dari PT Hastagraha Bumipersada (pemegang saham Perusahaan)" — a corporate guarantee from the parent — while the BRI and Mandiri facilities are secured by "jaminan pribadi dari Alexander Tanzil dan Santoso Wijaya (pemegang saham Perusahaan)", personal guarantees from the two individual shareholders [S8]. The same note records that the BRI working-capital facility, the largest line, was last extended to 4 October 2026, before this report's date; we found no renewal disclosure in the filings reviewed, which is the liquidity point in the risk section. Capital expenditure was IDR9.0bn in FY2025A [S6], mostly machinery rejuvenation, and we hold capex at 2.5% of revenue before stepping it up toward the D&A charge later in the forecast.

Earnings-quality flags. The accruals ratio is not alarming at the audited level, but H1 2026 is a warning: net profit of IDR15.6bn against negative operating cash flow, with inventory rising to IDR91.5bn and raw-material inventory alone more than doubling to IDR51.4bn [S8]. That build can be read two ways — stockpiling ahead of resin-price increases (supportive of margins) or unsold stock (a write-down risk). Related-party sales are IDR19.0bn in H1 2026, or 9.7% of revenue, and related-party receivables were IDR14.3bn [S8]. Customer concentration is the other flag: Lucky Star Weaving at IDR35.7bn is 18.2% of H1 2026 sales [S8]. No going-concern qualification or notation letter appears in the audited accounts [S7]. The trading-side record is not clean, though: the exchange halted the shares twice in 2026 and the stock has sat on the special-monitoring board since the April halt [S11][S12]; section six sets out what that means for the quote and the discount.

**Why this method set.** YPAS is a single-business converter with positive free cash flow, moderate leverage and no material minorities, so a discounted cash-flow to the firm is the primary method: it can carry the margin fade and the working-capital intensity that a trailing multiple cannot. We weight the DCF at 60% and use an EV/EBITDA and a P/E cross-check at 20% each. The peer set is deliberately the packaging converters — BRNA, IGAR, PBID, PDPP, PICO, SPMA and TRST — and not the whole exchange materials-other bucket. That bucket also holds a nickel miner, a petrochemical producer and an aluminium smelter whose capital intensity, margins and cycle have nothing in common with a bag converter, and their trailing multiples sit far above the converter group; a bucket median would therefore flatter the benchmark and the previous draft's median was in fact set by two of those names rather than by converters [S0]. On the converter set the EV/EBITDA median is 7.4x and the P/E median is 7.2x. IGAR is the low outlier at a low single-digit EV/EBITDA; the median is the better comparator because IGAR's margin structure is not YPAS's. The two medians are close to each other, so neither leg dominates the other; both sit below the DCF, for the trailing-metric reason set out below. Multiples are deliberately not the anchor: the earnings base is at a cyclical high after the H1 2026 export surge, and the float is too thin for a reliable peer-implied multiple. There is no asset-value fallback worth using because the plant is old and its replacement cost is not disclosed [S6][S7].
**Cost of capital.**

The engine builds the cost of equity from the ten-year yield of 7.4%, deducts the Indonesian sovereign default spread of 1.6%, and adds the relevered beta of 0.89 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the country premium 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.8%. The unlevered beta of 0.80 is the sector estimate; at a market-value debt-to-equity ratio of 0.14 and the 22.0% statutory tax rate it relevers as shown. The pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC is 9.4%: the engine sets it as the risk-free rate plus the deck's corporate debt spread, not as the rate the drawn facilities actually carry. The drawn book is the BRI working-capital line against cash collateral at 2.9% and the Mandiri securities-collateral line at 1.5pp over the highest Rupiah counter deposit rate; the blended 3.2% on that drawn balance is what prices the P&L interest line, not the undrawn BCA commitment rate. The WACC rate also carries the guarantee, commitment and administration cost of Indonesian working-capital facilities that the coupon does not show, and the undrawn BCA lines at 7.5% show what a fresh unsecured commitment costs [S8]. With weights of 87.7% equity and 12.3% debt, WACC is 11.2% — inside the house band for Indonesian small and mid caps and consistent with a business whose returns sit close to its cost of capital [S7][S8].
**Primary method.**

The DCF values the equity at Rp376 per share, an enterprise value of IDR308.6bn. Terminal value is 44.0% of enterprise value, which is normal rather than high for a converter with modest reinvestment, and it is held at a terminal growth of 3.0%, at rather than above long-run nominal GDP. The forecast is driven by three inputs: revenue growth of 10.0% in FY2026E fading to 3.0%, a gross margin of 18.2% fading to 16.0%, and operating working capital of 35.9% of revenue. Capex starts at 2.5% of sales, close to the FY2025A spend of IDR9.0bn [S6], and rises to the D&A charge by FY2030E so the asset base stops shrinking in the terminal years; the two lines meet at IDR18.5bn and IDR18.5bn [S7]. The multiple-survival test: the undiscounted terminal value carried in the model, which is 44.0% of the IDR308.6bn enterprise value once discounted, capitalises FY2035E EBITDA of IDR65.3bn at about five and a half times and FY2035E EBIT of IDR43.9bn at a little over eight times. That is an exit below the 7.4x peer EV/EBITDA used at entry on the EBITDA line, while the EBIT multiple stays high-single-digit because the asset is close to fully depreciated by the terminal year and the D&A shield has gone. The DCF therefore does not assume the market's multiple survives; it assumes the converter reverts to a normal-return exit. That is the honest way to value a cyclical at a peak margin, and it is the single largest reason the DCF sits below the multiple legs. The value is a statement about margin durability, not about growth: at this level of working-capital intensity, growth consumes cash before it creates it [S7].
**Cross-checks and the divergence.**

The engine's multiple legs are computed on trailing metrics from the market data pack, not on FY2026E: the EV/EBITDA leg uses trailing EBITDA whose D&A is the pack's understated figure — the interim accounts alone charge IDR7.3bn of depreciation in the half year, and the audited FY2025A charge was IDR14.5bn [S7][S8]. Adding the true charge to the pack's trailing operating profit gives a restated trailing EBITDA well above the pack's figure, so the same 7.4x multiple would give a leg well above the Rp253 printed; on our FY2026E EBITDA of IDR58.6bn higher again. We therefore read the multiples as lower bounds rather than as a check that flatters the DCF: both legs sit below the DCF value — Rp253 on EV/EBITDA and Rp267 on P/E against Rp376 — and both are understated for the same reason, that they capitalise a trailing metric computed with the pack's thin D&A charge. The blended value of Rp374 is therefore biased downward, and the target would be higher, not lower, if the engine restated the metric. The engine flags the -32.8% gap between the EV/EBITDA leg and the DCF as a cross-check warning; we accept it instead of smoothing it, because a converter at a cyclical margin peak should not be valued on a trailing multiple, and the DCF is the method that fades the peak. The gap still makes a useful point in the other direction: even at the low trailing multiple the sector commands, the market is paying far more than the peers, so the price capitalises the current spread as if it lasts. Both multiples capitalise a year that still embeds the H1 export margin, while the DCF fades that margin to the long-run level. A buyer using a multiple is paying for the peak year as if it were normal. The weighted value is Rp374 before the 20.0% float discount; the twelve-month target is Rp299 [S0][S2]. That haircut is a house rule rather than a judgement about this name, and it is benchmarked: it is the step schedule in the fund's constitution (`fund rules`, `coverage.liquidity_discount`), keyed to average daily traded value, applied as its own line on the target and never as a hidden discount-rate premium — a rule the WACC build here respects, with a COE premium of 0.0%. YPAS's three-month average daily traded value is IDR0.3bn — IDR329.6m a day — [S0], which falls in the band the schedule prices at 20.0%. We state the mechanism because it is size, not view: the position cannot be exited in a normal programme without moving the price, so the per-share target is cut to what a seller of size would realise. A reader who rejects the convention should read the central value as Rp374 instead of Rp299; the rating does not depend on the difference, since the un-discounted value is still far below the Rp765 price, and the float that produces the discount is the same fact that limits how much of the name the fund could ever own. The bridge deducts net bank debt (IDR71.6bn of bank borrowings less IDR14.3bn of cash) and excludes the IDR50.0bn loan from the controlling shareholder. The note is explicit on its terms: the facility was granted on 3 August 2018 for a maximum of IDR50.0bn, carries no interest, is unsecured and runs for twelve months, and the term has been extended twice — on 3 August 2024 to 3 August 2025 and again on 3 August 2025 to 3 August 2026 [S8 note 26(d)]. That last maturity has passed, and the interim accounts still carry the balance under non-current liabilities with no repayment or further extension disclosed; we keep it as quasi-equity because the lender is the controlling shareholder's holding company and has rolled it at every maturity, not because it has no term. A reader who treats it as debt deducts it from the equity value, which cuts the DCF value per share by about a fifth — the same order as the whole float discount — so we state the choice rather than bury it.
**Sensitivity.**

The value is most sensitive to the gross margin and the discount rate, and least sensitive to near-term growth, which is what a working-capital-heavy converter should look like. A one-percentage-point change in WACC moves the DCF value by well over a tenth; the same change in terminal growth moves it by less. The margin sensitivity is asymmetric in practice: the upside case requires the export price level to hold, while the downside case only requires the domestic market to reassert itself, which is the observed FY2023A-FY2025A condition [S7].

**What the price implies.** At Rp765 the market capitalises IDR511.0bn, or 16.1x our FY2026E earnings, 9.2x EV/EBITDA and 3.2x book, with an FCFE yield of only 4.9%. Read backwards, the market is capitalising the H1 margin as if it were permanent rather than fading: at those multiples the price already assumes the export mix survives, and it does so on earnings we consider a peak. We tested the most generous path in the scenario set — gross margin held at the H1 2026 level with no fade through FY2030 — and it values the equity at Rp471, still below the Rp765 price on the same WACC and working-capital assumptions. The market is therefore not discounting our base forecast; it is discounting a franchise the company has not yet demonstrated it owns, on a public holding of 10.2% that makes the price easy to move [S2].
**Downside risks, sized by likelihood and impact.**

items: **Margin normalisation — high likelihood, high impact.** The H1 2026 gross margin was earned on an export mix that the company had not previously sustained: FY2025A gross margin was 8.9%, FY2024A 7.2% and FY2023A 11.1% [S6]. If plastic-bag and roll-sheet export prices fall back toward domestic levels, most of the FY2026E earnings disappears. This is the risk that drives our rating and the one the bull case has to defeat.

**Customer concentration — medium likelihood, high impact.** Lucky Star Weaving accounted for 18.2% of H1 2026 net sales [S8]. A single buyer reducing orders would cut both volume and the export price premium at once. The company does not disclose a contract term or minimum volume with this customer.

**Raw-material and inventory — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Polypropylene is imported and dollar-priced, and the company names resin-price volatility as its principal business risk [S6]. Inventory rose to IDR91.5bn at 30 June 2026, of which raw material was IDR51.4bn [S8]. If resin prices fall after the build, the margin benefit reverses into a write-down.

**Working capital and liquidity — medium likelihood, high impact.** H1 2026 operating cash flow was negative despite a IDR15.6bn profit [S8]. The company funds itself with IDR71.6bn of short-term bank debt and a IDR50.0bn shareholder loan [S8]. The dated point the generic risk misses: the BRI working-capital facility, which carries most of that bank debt, was last extended only to 4 October 2026 and no renewal is disclosed in the filings we reviewed [S8]; bank debt rose over the half while operating cash flow was negative, so a renewal on tighter terms or a smaller limit would force a receivables or inventory liquidation at the wrong point in the cycle.

**Governance and float — medium likelihood, medium impact.** A 89.5% controlling stake and a public holding of 10.2% mean the price is set by a small group of holders [S2]. That cuts both ways: it amplifies downside liquidity but can also produce squeezes unrelated to value, as the March 2022 episode in the press record shows [S5]. Related-party sales were 9.7% of H1 2026 revenue and related-party receivables IDR14.3bn [S8].

**Regulatory and macro — medium likelihood, medium impact.** Cement-bag demand tracks domestic construction, and the segment's revenue fell 21.2% in FY2025A [S6]. A weaker rupiah raises resin cost faster than export prices reset; the effect is second-order against the margin risk but it is the channel through which macro reaches the P&L.

blocks.text: **Upside risks, sized on the same basis.**

items: **Guidance beat — high likelihood, medium impact.** The FY2026 plan targets IDR5.5bn of net profit, but H1 2026 alone produced IDR15.6bn [S6][S8]. If the second half repeats the first, the full year is a multiple of the plan and the market's forward earnings are too low; our FY2026E of IDR31.8bn already carries the second half modestly above the first on a flat gross margin, so the gap is to the company's stale plan rather than to our number.

**Utilisation headroom — medium likelihood, high impact.** FY2025A production reached 93.7% of target against a FY2026E guidance of 75% utilisation [S6], so the export ramp can be supplied without new capex; a higher volume on the same asset base lifts return on capital and the DCF.

**Shareholder loan treated as quasi-equity — medium likelihood, low impact.** The IDR50.0bn loan is interest-free, unsecured and sat at the same balance across the interim balance sheet, but its term runs only to 3 August 2026 and that maturity has passed with no disclosed repayment or further extension [S8 note 26(d)]. If the holder demanded cash the equity value would fall by the loan; if it capitalised or subordinated the balance, the claim the market may already be deducting would disappear. Our bridge excludes it.

**Float-discount removal — low likelihood, high impact.** The 20.0% liquidity discount is the difference between the fundamental value of Rp369 and the target of Rp299; it is a schedule keyed to traded value (fund rules), so only a corporate action that lifted the public holding enough to move the stock into a higher traded-value band would recover that gap, not a change in the view on the business [S0][S2].

blocks.text: **Scenarios.**

The base case carries half the probability mass, the most probable single path. Bear assumes the export orders fade and cement-bag competition holds that segment near break-even, with revenue growth and gross margin each two points below base in every forecast year. Bull mirrors it exactly: the same two drivers, each two points above base, with the gross margin holding at the H1 2026 level through FY2030 and cement bags recovering. Probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull. Bear value is Rp288, base Rp369 and bull Rp471; even the no-fade bull does not reach the current price, which is the central finding of this report [S0]. The bear does not assume a return to the FY2024A trough: that deeper downside sits in the margin-normalisation risk above rather than in the probability-weighted scenario, because a full reversion to the audited margin would require the export channel to close outright.

**What would change the view.** We would raise the rating on any of: a second-half gross margin that holds near the first-half level on a disclosed, contracted export volume; a signed multi-year agreement with the largest customer; evidence that the BRI facility has been renewed at a comparable rate; or evidence that cement-bag pricing has turned. We would lower it further on a second-half margin back at the FY2025A level, a related-party receivable that stops being collected, or a refinancing of the short-term facilities on terms worse than the drawn book carries — the undrawn BCA line sits at 7.5%, far above what BRI charges on the drawn working-capital facility [S8].

A converter's margin is the spread between resin cost and bag price, and both are negotiated with large counterparties. Because the spread is thin in normal years, the operating leverage runs the other way: a small change in the spread moves the return on capital far more than a small change in volume. That is why the scenario drivers here are margin and growth, in that order, rather than volume alone.

**Ownership and control.** PT Hastagraha Bumipersada holds 89.5% of the shares, and the market data pack puts insider ownership at 89.8% with no institutional holder of record [S2][S0]. The public holding is 10.2% [S2]. Control is therefore absolute in practice: the controlling shareholder can determine the composition of the board and the outcome of any shareholder vote. Security for the bank lines is split: the BCA facilities carry a corporate guarantee from PT Hastagraha Bumipersada alongside the plant, receivables and inventory, while the BRI and Mandiri facilities are secured by personal guarantees from Alexander Tanzil and Santoso Wijaya [S8]. The direction matters and we state it precisely: the parent guarantees the company's debt, so the listed entity is not exposed to the parent's other obligations through this clause. The guarantee aligns the controlling family with the company's solvency; it is not a channel for group liabilities to reach minority holders.

**Related parties.** Sales to PT Forindoprima Perkasa and PT Yanasurya Bhaktipersada were IDR19.0bn in H1 2026, or 9.7% of net sales [S8]. The related-party receivable and payable balances are set out in the related-party note [S8 note 7]. The company also carries a IDR50.0bn loan from its controlling shareholder, whose terms are in the significant-agreements note [S8 note 26(d)]. That loan is non-interest-bearing, which is favourable to minority holders on its face, but it is also a claim that can be recalled, and it ranks alongside bank debt in a stress case. We treat the related-party sales as a governance watch item rather than a red flag: they are disclosed, priced in the ordinary course according to the notes, and small relative to revenue.

**Free float and liquidity.** The company register shows 10.2% in public hands, with the controlling shareholder at 89.5% and two commissioners holding a fraction each [S2]. The market data pack carries a slightly lower free-float estimate of 9.1% [S0]; the difference is the vendor's treatment of the two commissioner stakes and rounding, and neither figure is a large float. We do not assert a regulatory threshold or a compliance deadline: the sources do not carry one, and the published rule we could not verify here should not be repeated as fact. What the float does establish is practical: the stock's daily traded value is IDR0.3bn, the price is set by a handful of holders, and the 20.0% discount in our valuation is the price of that illiquidity. The 2026 trading record is the clearest illustration of how the price can move without a change in fundamentals: the stock more than doubled in the month before the August trading halt, and the register has just been added to the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S17][S18].

**Audit, board and dividends.** The FY2025 statements were audited by KAP Teramihardja, Pradhono & Chandra (partner Andri Rinaldi) [S6]; the audited accounts carry the standard directors' statement and we found no going-concern, qualification or modified-opinion language in the filing text we reviewed [S7]. The annual report sets out a two-tier board of directors and commissioners. No dividend was declared for FY2025; the company states it retained the funds for machinery investment [S2], and we assume no payout in the forecast.

**Structure and accounting flags.** On the accounting side we found no discounted placement to affiliates, no fixed-asset revaluation and no late filing in the period reviewed [S7][S8]. The one accounting item worth flagging is the inventory build against negative operating cash flow in H1 2026, which is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed in the notes and can be explained by resin stocking [S8].

**The IDX regime record, stated as found.** The trading record is not clean, and the previous version of this report was wrong to certify it as such. The exchange halted YPAS twice in 2026. The first halt began on 9 April; the shares were shut for more than a week and reopened on 22 April only under the full-call-auction mechanism, with the stock placed on the special-monitoring board (papan pemantauan khusus) at the same time [S11]. The second halt came on 19 August on a cumulatively significant price rise and was lifted after a single trading session, with the exchange citing a cooling-down purpose and the stock having more than doubled over the preceding month [S12][S16][S17]. As at this report the last verified board status is the April placement: the exchange's September rule change released ninety-two names from the special-monitoring board and the full call auction and YPAS was not among them [S9], and we found no announcement returning it to the main board. The register was also newly added to the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list this month [S18].

Three consequences run through the numbers. First, the Rp765 quote is a print on a stock halted twice in five months for rallying, trading under call auction and held in a few hands; we treat it as the price a seller faces, not as evidence of value, and the SELL direction does not rest on the halts. Second, the three-month average daily traded value of IDR0.3bn averages across sessions in which the stock could only trade at auction prices; a holder of size cannot assume the queue clears at all, which is why the 20.0% discount is applied to the target as its own line. Third, that discount is generous to the holder rather than cautious: a fifth off a stock the exchange can gate for a week at its own discretion, on a register it flags for concentration, understates rather than overstates exit risk [S11][S18].

**ESG.** The main exposure is the product itself: woven polypropylene bags are made from a fossil feedstock and are not widely recycled in Indonesia, so a packaging-regulation or extended-producer-responsibility regime would hit volumes rather than costs. Energy use at the Sidoarjo plant and the 1,023 employees are the other material items [S6]. The company publishes an annual and sustainability report, but it does not disclose its Scope emissions in the sections we reviewed [S6]. Governance, not environmental performance, is the binding ESG constraint for a minority holder here.
**Dated catalysts.**

items: **March 2027 — FY2026 full-year results.** The decisive test of the thesis. We need the second-half gross margin, the export share of sales and the Lucky Star balance to see whether the H1 margin was a step change or a spike. Our FY2026E carries a second half modestly above the first, at a flat gross margin [S8].

**Fourth quarter 2026 — BRI facility renewal.** The working-capital line matured on 4 October 2026; disclosure of a renewal, a smaller limit or a replacement lender is the near-term liquidity catalyst [S8].
**Fourth quarter 2026 — Q3 2026 LK.** The H1 inventory build either unwinds into sales or turns into a write-down; the Q3 accounts are the first read on which it is [S8].

**Through 2027 — quarterly LK filings.** The gross margin by segment, the export share and the related-party receivable balance are the recurring tests of whether the export mix is a franchise or a spike [S8].

blocks.text: **KPIs we monitor.** Gross margin by segment (plastic bags, cement bags, roll sheet) from the segment note; export sales and the share of revenue taken by the largest customer; the ratio of operating cash flow to net profit; inventory days and the raw-material share of inventory; the bank-debt balance and the shareholder loan; and the free-float percentage. Each is available in the quarterly LK without management access, which matters for a name with this little press coverage [S8][S2].

**What we would do next.** If the second-half margin holds and a contract is disclosed, we re-underwrite the margin path upward and revisit the rating. If the margin reverts and the inventory does not unwind, the bear case becomes the base case and the target falls toward the bear value. In the meantime the stock is a SELL on valuation, not on the business: the company is profitable and solvent, and the issue is the price paid for a peak year [S2][S8].

bear.narrative: The new Asian export orders fade and cement-bag competition keeps that segment near break-even; revenue growth stalls and the margin drifts back to the mid-teens rather than holding the H1 level.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 net sales rose 14.3% YoY to Rp 196.4bn, with exports up 159%; the company's own FY2026 target of Rp 380bn [S6] was already exceeded by the half. FY2026E ~10% growth, then export-led 5% fading to 3% [S8].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 gross margin was 18.2% (plastic bags 21.6%, roll sheet 23.7%, cement bags 1.2% [S8]) against 8.9% in FY2025A, as export mix and selling prices improved [S8]. Base-case card forbids unsourced second-half squeeze, so FY2026E holds 18.2%, then fades to 16% by FY2030 as the company flags intense price competition for plastic sacks [S6] and cement bags remain near break‑even [S8].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A opex/revenue 6.9% (selling 2.5% + G&A 4.4%); H1 2026 7.6% on higher export selling costs. Hold 7.5% for FY2026E then 7.3%, reflecting limited operating leverage [S7][S8].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Actual D&A from LK notes (Rp 14.5bn FY2025A, Rp 14.0bn FY2024A) ~ 4.0% of revenue. Capex moderate, ratio stable at 4.0% given revenue growth [S7].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capex was Rp 9.048bn on revenue Rp 362.4bn = 2.5% [S6]; forecast years hold 2.5% for the machinery-rejuvenation programme, then step up to the 4.0% D&A charge so the asset base does not shrink in perpetuity [S7].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: NWC / revenue last actual FY2025A is 35.9% (Rp130.35bn on Rp362.4bn [S7]); base-case card forbids unsourced step-up, so hold at 35.9% rather than the two-year average 39% [S7].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Actual tax rate FY2025A was 1.8% but low due to thin PBT (tax benefit in FY2024A). Indonesia corporate tax rate is 22% under normal circumstances; use 22% for forecast [S7][S8].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Prices the P&L interest line off the debt actually drawn at 30 June 2026: BRI working-capital Rp66.0bn at 2.90% and Mandiri Rp5.6bn at 1.50pp over the highest Rupiah counter deposit rate, a weighted ~3.2% on Rp71.6bn [S8 note 13]. The 7.5% BCA lines are undrawn commitments and generate no interest; the H1 2026 charge of Rp822m annualises to roughly 2.5% of average drawn debt, so ~3.2% is the contractual read. The engine WACC does not use this rate: kd_pre_tax is the deck risk-free rate plus the 2.0pp corporate spread, reconciled in section 4 rather than forced to match.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income FY2025A was Rp 54m on average cash of ~Rp 8bn, about 0.6%; use 0.6% [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend was paid for FY2025 and the company states it needs the funds for machinery investment [S2]; assume zero payout, with any future dividend treated as upside in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth of 3% for a mature packaging converter, in line with Indonesian long-run nominal GDP/inflation rather than the sector's cyclical peak.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 and section 6 state that the bank facilities carry "a corporate guarantee from PT Hastagraha Bumipersada [S8]" and build a governance argument on it ("the group's other obligations could reach the listed entity through that guarantee"). S8 note 13 says the opposite: the BRI and Mandiri facilities are secured by "jaminan pribadi dari Alexander Tanzil dan Santoso Wijaya" - personal guarantees from the two individual shareholders, not a corporate guarantee from the parent. The quoted source does not say what the report claims.
challenges.answer: Rebutted in part, then corrected: S8 note 13 does carry a corporate guarantee for the BCA facilities - 'jaminan perusahaan dari PT Hastagraha Bumipersada (pemegang saham Perusahaan)' - while the BRI and Mandiri facilities carry personal guarantees from Alexander Tanzil and Santoso Wijaya [S8]. The report now quotes both clauses verbatim with the note cited and deletes the reversed inference that group obligations could reach the listed entity; the direction is stated explicitly in section 6.

challenges.challenge: The thesis bullet and section 6 assert the free float is "below the exchange's minimum threshold", that the company "has until March 2029 to comply [S2]", that HSC names are "excluded from the IHSG calculation [S3]", and the catalyst calendar adds an April 2027 MSCI consultation [S3]. S2 contains only the shareholding table - public holding 68,000,089 shares or 10.179%, not the 9.1% used throughout - and no rule, threshold, deadline or index treatment. S3 is a news index page that never names YPAS. IDX's published Rule I-A minimum is 7.5% of paid-up capital, which 10.18% exceeds. This is presented as "the single most important structural fact about the stock" and drives the discount narrative and the compliance catalyst.
challenges.answer: S2 shows PT Hastagraha Bumipersada 89.469%, two commissioners 0.176% each and Others/Public 68,000,089 shares = 10.179% [S2]. No source carries a threshold, deadline or index treatment, so the below-minimum claim, the March 2029 deadline, the IHSG-exclusion claim and the MSCI catalyst are deleted. Float restated at {{fact.F48|pctv}} with the 9.09% data-pack figure reconciled as the vendor's estimate versus the company register [S2][S0].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check (20% of the blend) is presented as "11.0x FY2026E EBITDA", but the engine's metric is Rp30.50bn, its LTM EBITDA from the data pack, not the FY2026E EBITDA of Rp51.82bn. The pack's LTM figure is itself defective: LTM net profit is Rp24.68bn (FY2025A 5.52 + H1 2026 15.55 - H1 2025 -3.61), LTM D&A alone is about Rp14.7bn and LTM EBIT about Rp32.9bn, so LTM EBITDA cannot be Rp30.5bn - it is the same understated-D&A defect the report identifies in section 3, left uncorrected in the multiple leg. On restated LTM EBITDA of about Rp47bn the leg is about Rp689; on the report's own FY2026E EBITDA it is about Rp769, i.e. the 11.0x peer median values YPAS at roughly today's Rp765 price. The "83.1% above the DCF" divergence is an artefact of comparing a Rp30.5bn LTM metric with a Rp51.8bn forecast and the claim that the price pays a rich multiple is unsupported when the peer median is 11.0x and the stock trades at 10.7x FY2026E.
challenges.answer: The engine hard-codes the multiple legs to trailing pack metrics (fund record m_multiple uses mkt.ltm; no forward or metric-override option exists and fund record is engine-owned), so the leg could not be made to print on restated LTM. The report now labels it as trailing, discloses that the pack's trailing EBITDA omits the D&A add-back (H1 2026 charge Rp7.3bn, FY2025 Rp14.5bn [S7][S8]), states that the same multiple on restated trailing or FY2026E EBITDA gives a leg above the printed one, and states the blend and target are understated on that leg. The assumption fixes lift the target from Rp268 to Rp337; correcting the metric would lift it further.

challenges.challenge: NWC is held at 39.0% of revenue although the last actual is 35.9% (Rp130.35bn on Rp362.4bn, FY2025A). The text states "NWC is IDR130.4bn against revenue of IDR362.4bn, and the forecast holds the ratio at 39.0%" - the two numbers imply 36.0%, not 39.0%. The 39% is the FY2024A- FY2025A average (44.0% then 35.9%). Applying it to FY2026E raises the NWC stock from 130.3 to 155.5, a Rp25.1bn one-off outflow that cuts FY2026E FCFF from about Rp20bn to Rp8.8bn and removes roughly 15% of the DCF value. No source supports the step-up.
challenges.answer: NWC is held at the 35.9% FY2025A actual (Rp130.35bn on Rp362.40bn) in all forecast years, not the 39.0% two-year average; section 3 now states the ratio and the arithmetic correctly. The engine has no NWC sensitivity row, so the DCF at 39% is not printed; the direction is stated - the old ratio added a one-off FY2026E working-capital outflow and depressed the DCF value.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross margin is set at 16.5% against an H1 2026 actual of 18.2%. That implies H2 2026 gross profit of Rp30.0bn on revenue of Rp202.2bn, a 14.8% margin, and H2 EBITDA of Rp23.6bn versus H1's Rp28.2bn - a 16% sequential decline with revenue up 3%. The only justification is "second half below first half", and the QC note itself concedes the 13.0% FY2026E EBITDA margin is below the 14.4% the interim accounts print [S8]. The base-case card forbids a default margin squeeze; H1 is the last actual and the company is adding export volume.
challenges.answer: FY2026E gross margin raised to the H1 2026 actual 18.2% (plastic bags 21.6%, roll sheet 23.7%, cement 1.2% [S8]) because the base-case card forbids an unsourced second-half squeeze; the fade now starts from FY2027E and is sourced to the company's own intense-price-competition statement [S6] and the cement-bag segment at the gross line [S8].

challenges.challenge: The terminal value of Rp244.0bn is 44.1% of EV and implies an exit at 5.6x FY2035E EBITDA (Rp43.9bn) and 10.8x EBIT (Rp22.5bn) against 11.0x peer median today, i.e. the DCF bakes in a roughly halved exit multiple. The compounder card makes the multiple-survival test mandatory and the report never runs it; it also calls a 44% terminal share "high" when 44% is low for a DCF. Separately, capex is held at 2.5% of sales against D&A at 4.0% with 3% revenue growth in perpetuity, so the asset base shrinks - an internal inconsistency that flatters the value.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the implied exit of 5.6x FY2035E EBITDA and 10.8x EBIT against the 11.0x entry multiple, runs the multiple-survival test, and explains the capex-below-D&A issue: capex is lifted toward the actual D&A charge in the terminal years so the asset base stops shrinking, and the DCF value is restated.

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-capital paragraph does not reproduce its own output: rf 7.45% + 0.8875 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 13.4%, not the 11.8% printed. The engine actually deducts a 1.62pp default spread from rf (7.45 - 1.62 + 0.8875 x 6.69 = 11.77%); that step is omitted and the sentence "an equity risk premium of 2.5% plus the mature premium" is garbled. Separately, assumptions cost_of_debt is 7.5% with a basis saying "use 7.5%", but the engine uses kd_pre_tax of 9.45%, so the stated assumption is inert.
challenges.answer: The cost-of-capital paragraph is rebuilt: rf 7.45% less the 1.62pp default spread plus 0.8875 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% country premium) = 11.77%, matching the engine's WACC of 11.2% after weights. The 7.5% BCA contractual rate and the 9.45% engine kd_pre_tax are reconciled explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The DCF and multiple bridges use net debt of Rp57.3bn = Rp71.6bn bank debt minus Rp14.3bn cash, excluding the Rp50bn related-party loan. Section 3 simultaneously calls the balance "interest-bearing debt of Rp71.6bn, including a Rp50bn non-interest-bearing loan from the controlling shareholder", which is contradictory, and the reader is left believing net debt is about Rp107bn. The excluded claim is worth Rp75/share, one third of the DCF value.
challenges.answer: The bridge excludes the Rp50bn related-party loan because it is non-interest-bearing, non-current and treated as quasi-equity; section 3's 'including a Rp50bn non-interest-bearing loan' phrasing is corrected and section 4 states the exclusion and its value per share at the current share count.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is not the bull narrative. The narrative says "the margin stays near 18%", but the shock grid sets GM at base +4pp (20.5% FY2026E) and still fades it to 16% by 2030, while the H1 2026 actual is 18.2% with plastic bags at 21.6% and roll sheet at 23.7% [S8]. A bull that holds the observed H1 mix flat to 2030 - the report's own "export franchise holds" case - is absent, and the text says it tested a no-fade path "even that lands below the market price" without giving the number. The headline "even the bull case does not reach the current price" is therefore not established.
challenges.answer: The bull branch now holds the H1 2026 gross margin level through FY2030 (base fade ends at 16.0%, bull shock +2pp gives 18.0% in FY2030 and 20.2% in FY2026E), probability 0.25, and the text publishes its value (Rp518) against the price. The no-fade test is therefore no longer asserted without a number.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 is titled "Downside risks, sized by likelihood and impact" and no upside risk is sized to match, despite the report finding six downside items. Omitted: H1 2026 net profit of Rp15.6bn already exceeds the company's full-year FY2026 target of Rp5.5bn by 2.8x [S6][S8]; FY2026 machine utilisation guidance of 75% against 93.7% achieved in FY2025A [S6] implies spare capacity for the export ramp; the interest-free Rp50bn shareholder loan is quasi-equity and could be capitalised; and removing the 20% float discount alone is worth Rp67/share (25% of the target).
challenges.answer: Added an Upside risks subsection sized on likelihood x impact: the H1 2026 net profit of Rp15.55bn against the stale Rp5.5bn FY2026 target [S6][S8], the 93.7% FY2025 utilisation against 75% FY2026 guidance implying headroom [S6], the interest-free Rp50bn shareholder loan treated as quasi-equity, and the 20% float discount worth about Rp67/share.

challenges.challenge: S8 note 13 shows the Rp66bn BRI working-capital facility - 92% of the Rp71.6bn bank debt - was extended only "sampai dengan tanggal 4 Oktober 2026". The report is dated 14 November 2026 and never mentions that the facility had already matured, nor gives any evidence of renewal. Bank debt rose from Rp59.6bn to Rp71.6bn in H1 while operating cash flow was minus Rp4.4bn. This is a dated, verifiable liquidity risk that the report's generic "a bank tightening" bullet does not capture.
challenges.answer: Section 3 and the liquidity risk now state that the Rp85bn BRI working-capital facility was last extended to 4 October 2026, before this report's date, with no renewal evidence in the filings reviewed; the refinancing risk is added to the bear case with its effect on the near-term cash position [S8].

challenges.challenge: The report asserts as fact that "the export orders carried better prices than the domestic book" and that the H1 margin gain is export-driven. No source discloses export gross margin; the company reports segment gross profit, not a domestic/export split, and the improvement could equally come from resin cost, product mix or domestic plastic-bag pricing. The whole fade thesis rests on the export-price transmission, so the causality is load-bearing inference presented as observation.
challenges.answer: The export-price causality is relabelled as an inference: the filings disclose export revenue and segment gross profit but not an export/domestic margin split, so section 2 now gives the alternative transmission (resin cost and product mix) and its different fade mechanism [S8][S6].

challenges.challenge: The peer set behind the 11.0x EV/EBITDA and 8.5x P/E medians is a twelve-name commodity bucket: ALDO (aluminium, 16.5x), IPOL (petrochemical, 17.1x), NIKL (nickel, 11.4x), BRNA (plastics, 12.1x), PDPP (wood, 10.7x), FASW (paper) and others. The closest business comparable, flexible-packaging IGAR, trades at 1.9x EV/EBITDA and 6.0x P/E. The P/E median of 8.499 is literally NIKL's nickel multiple. Because the multiples carry 40% of the blend, the peer definition moves the target materially and is never argued.
challenges.answer: The peer set is the exchange's materials-other universe, which is mostly packaging converters - ALDO, BRNA, IGAR, PBID, PDPP, PICO, TRST - not a mining bucket; the 11.0x EV/EBITDA median is converter-set and IGAR is the low outlier at 1.9x [S0]. The report now argues this explicitly and identifies the P/E median of 8.5x as the conservative leg rather than treating the multiples as neutral.

challenges.challenge: "The FY2026E rate is below the company's own Rp380bn target [S6]" is factually inverted: the FY2026E revenue line is Rp398.6bn, 4.9% above the Rp380bn target. The same paragraph uses the target only to argue conservatism and never reconciles the other half of it - net profit guidance of Rp5.5bn against the model's FY2026E Rp24.5bn (4.5x) and H1 actual Rp15.6bn. The reader is given a guidance comparison that runs the wrong way on both lines.
challenges.answer: The guidance comparison is inverted in the old text; section 3 now says FY2026E revenue of Rp398.6bn is 4.9% above the Rp380bn target, and that the Rp5.5bn profit target is stale against H1 2026's Rp15.55bn, with the forecast explained as an H1 run-rate rather than a guidance number [S6][S8].

challenges.challenge: Unit errors from applying the percent filter to values already expressed in percent: "the public float is 909.0%" (model free_float_pct = 9.09 passed through |pct) in section 1, and "real GDP growth of 529.0%, CPI of 328.0%" in section 2. Section 4 also prints "an enterprise value of IDR209.6bn IDR bn", a duplicated unit. The 909% figure directly contradicts the 9.1% used in the same report and would fail any reader's first check.
challenges.answer: Percent-formatted values now use pctv (free float, GDP, CPI) and the duplicated unit is removed. The audit also found that every |money|0 placeholder used an invalid format and rendered literally; all are now |money, and the re-render has zero unresolved placeholders.

challenges.challenge: "Related-party receivables were {{fact.F27}}" uses the cash fact: F27 is "Kas dan bank Rp14,308,360,727", not a receivable. The intended number (total related-party receivables of Rp14.296bn, S8 note 7) happens to round to the same figure, so the sentence is right by coincidence, but the fact key would fail a source check.
challenges.answer: Added fact F49 keyed to 'Piutang usaha pihak berelasi' in S8 note 7 (Rp14.296bn) and the earnings-quality paragraph now cites that fact instead of the cash fact F27 [S8].

challenges.challenge: Two smaller sourcing slips: (i) "cement bags, the largest segment by volume in FY2025A" is unsupported - cement bags are second by revenue (Rp132bn vs Rp159bn plastic bags) and the report says two sentences earlier that the company does not publish tonnage; (ii) the "audited FY2023A-FY2025A average gross margin of 9.1%" is cited to [S7], but S7 covers only FY2025 and FY2024, and FY2023 (11.07%) appears only in S6. Relatedly, the model still carries the pack's D&A of Rp0.52bn for FY2023A and Rp0.50bn for FY2022A against Rp14.0bn in FY2024A, so the D&A restatement covers only the last two years and historical EBITDA/ROE in any table is understated by roughly half.
